patient.chief_complaint: Cognitive decline over two years and a lobar haemorrhage on anticoagulation, with the family asking whether the apixaban should continue
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Teresa Marchi is an 81-year-old retired pharmacist's assistant who attends with her daughter. Fourteen months ago, while established on apixaban for permanent atrial fibrillation, she sustained a left occipital lobar intracerebral haemorrhage which left her with a dense right hemianopia. The anticoagulant was stopped for six weeks and then restarted on the grounds of her stroke risk. Her daughter reports two years of cognitive decline that preceded the haemorrhage and has continued since: slowness, difficulty organising, forgetting conversations unless reminded of the setting, and loss of the ability to manage her own medication and money. She has fallen twice in the past year without head injury. Her blood pressure has been consistently well controlled around 130/75. Her father died of an intracerebral haemorrhage at 79. The daughter's explicit question is whether the apixaban should be continued, and she reports that no-one has been able to give her a clear answer. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation in alertness and no dream enactment.

findings.location: Strictly lobar: bilateral occipital, bilateral parietal, left temporal, right frontal cortical-subcortical junction

signal_characteristics.SWI: Seventeen rounded foci of signal loss at the cortical-subcortical junction, with no deep grey, no brainstem and no cerebellar microbleed

findings.location: Bilateral parietal and right frontal convexities, four separate sulci

signal_characteristics.SWI: Curvilinear cortical surface hypointensity in four separate sulci — disseminated siderosis

signal_characteristics.T2_FLAIR: Cavitated lesion with a gliotic rim involving the striate cortex

findings.type: White matter hyperintensity of presumed vascular origin

signal_characteristics.T2_FLAIR: Posteriorly weighted periventricular and subcortical hyperintensity

signal_characteristics.T2: Multiple centrum semiovale perivascular spaces with sparing of the basal ganglia

findings.location: Mild global, posterior weighting; medial temporal lobes preserved

volumetrics.white_matter_lesion_volume: Estimated 19 mL, Fazekas 2 with posterior predominance

additional_observations: Seventeen strictly lobar microbleeds with disseminated cortical superficial siderosis and a prior lobar haemorrhage: probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy by the Boston criteria version 2.0, at the severe end of the spectrum
No deep, brainstem or cerebellar microbleed, which excludes hypertensive arteriopathy as the explanation
Disseminated siderosis in four sulci is the single strongest imaging predictor of recurrent lobar haemorrhage
Centrum semiovale perivascular spaces with basal ganglia sparing and posteriorly weighted white matter change are supportive markers
mri.impression: Severe probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy by the Boston criteria version 2.0: seventeen strictly lobar microbleeds, disseminated cortical superficial siderosis in four sulci, and a prior lobar haemorrhage sustained on anticoagulation. The cognitive syndrome is a vascular cognitive disorder on this substrate, and the imaging burden places the recurrent haemorrhage risk at the top of the range.

CMP.clinical_significance: Not on a vitamin K antagonist; coagulation intrinsically normal

labs.interpretation: Renal function at eGFR 54 with age and weight supports the reduced apixaban dose. Coagulation is intrinsically normal. Lipids at target. TSH, B12, folate, RPR and HIV normal or negative, excluding reversible causes of the cognitive decline.

quantitative_data.adaptations: visually dependent tasks replaced with oral equivalents because of the hemianopia

specialized_test.impression: Executive dysfunction and slowed processing with preserved recognition memory, tested with oral equivalents to avoid confounding by the hemianopia, and informant-rated loss of instrumental independence.

findings.performance: Digit span backwards 0/1, serial sevens 2/3 — impaired

clinical_assessment.impression: MoCA 19/30 with an executive and retrieval profile and lost instrumental independence, on a background of a lobar haemorrhage and a dense hemianopia. The cognitive decline predated the haemorrhage, which points to a chronic vascular process rather than to the single event.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.query: vascular cognitive impairment diagnostic criteria and secondary prevention

results.title: Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement
results.authors: Sachdev P, Kalaria R, O'Brien J, et al.
results.summary: Requires a cognitive syndrome documented on a validated instrument plus imaging or temporal evidence that cerebrovascular disease accounts for it.

results.title: Neuroimaging standards for research into small vessel disease (STRIVE-2)
results.authors: Duering M, Biessels GJ, Brodtmann A, et al.
results.summary: Defines and standardises the reporting of white matter hyperintensity, lacunes, microbleeds, perivascular spaces and cortical superficial siderosis.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

medication_review.proposed: review of the current medication list for anticholinergic burden
warnings: Anticholinergic load is a reversible contributor to cognitive impairment in this population and should be quantified before any new prescription.
medication_review.summary: No prohibitive interaction identified within the current list.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment of dementia severity due to severe probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy (Boston criteria v2.0), with a prior anticoagulation-associated lobar haemorrhage and coexisting atrial fibrillation

differential.key_features: The default attribution for intracerebral haemorrhage, but her blood pressure has been well controlled for years and all seventeen microbleeds are strictly lobar with no deep or infratentorial lesion — the distribution excludes it

differential.diagnosis: Anticoagulation as the sole cause of the haemorrhage
differential.key_features: Apixaban was the proximate trigger, but a drug does not create seventeen lobar microbleeds and disseminated siderosis; it unmasked an underlying amyloid angiopathy, and that distinction is what determines whether it should be restarted

Amyloid angiopathy and Alzheimer's disease frequently coexist, but recall is cue-responsive, the hippocampi are preserved, and a biomarker would not change the management determined by the haemorrhage risk

differential.diagnosis: Post-haemorrhagic cognitive impairment from the occipital lesion alone
differential.key_features: The decline predated the haemorrhage by two years and the profile is executive rather than visual-associative
Fazekas 2 posteriorly weighted change is a supportive amyloid marker rather than a primary subcortical ischaemic burden

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a collateral history from an informant who sees the patient daily: the shape of the decline (abrupt, stepwise or gradual), whether any step can be dated to a cerebrovascular event, and which instrumental activities have been lost
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Two years of progressive executive decline predating a lobar haemorrhage that occurred on anticoagulation in a well-controlled hypertensive, with recurrent falls and a family history of fatal haemorrhage

optimal_actions.action: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MoCA 19/30 with an executive and retrieval profile and lost instrumental independence, with decline predating the haemorrhage

optimal_actions.action: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c, lipid panel)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible causes excluded; renal function documented as relevant to anticoagulant dosing, with intrinsically normal coagulation

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms — FLAIR for white matter hyperintensity with a Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for lacunes, DWI to establish that the lesions are chronic, and SWI for microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis — together with the medial temporal atrophy grade
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Seventeen strictly lobar microbleeds with disseminated cortical superficial siderosis and a prior lobar haemorrhage on anticoagulation — severe probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy, the highest-risk imaging phenotype for recurrence

optimal_actions.action: Order formal multi-domain neuropsychological testing to settle the executive-versus-amnestic attribution and to document a baseline for follow-up
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Executive and retrieval profile with preserved recognition, and formal documentation of the functional loss that establishes dementia severity

optimal_actions.action: Confirm the diagnostic criteria applied and the current secondary-prevention targets against the guidelines
optimal_actions.expected_finding: VASCOG 2014 criteria and the 2021 AHA/ASA secondary prevention targets confirmed

optimal_actions.action: Review the medication list for anticholinergic burden and for the interaction between antithrombotic choice and the microbleed burden before prescribing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticholinergic contributors identified and the antithrombotic choice reconciled with the imaging burden

optimal_actions.action: Answer the question the family has been asking: in severe probable amyloid angiopathy with a prior anticoagulation-associated lobar haemorrhage, disseminated cortical superficial siderosis and seventeen lobar microbleeds, the recurrent haemorrhage risk exceeds the embolic benefit — stop the apixaban, refer for assessment for left atrial appendage occlusion as the alternative for stroke prevention, maintain blood pressure below 130 mmHg systolic as the one intervention that reduces both risks, address the falls, and document the decision and its reasoning explicitly in the record
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticoagulation stopped on an explicit risk assessment, an alternative route to stroke prevention referred, blood pressure maintained at target, falls addressed, and the reasoning documented so the decision is not silently reversed again

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis and its mechanism to the patient and the informant, and address driving, medication management, finances, advance care planning and caregiver support
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and informant engaged in care planning; safety domains addressed

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture in an anticoagulated patient with severe probable amyloid angiopathy adds procedural and bleeding risk while the diagnosis is already established on imaging criteria and CSF cannot separate vascular from parenchymal amyloid

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Establish that the cognitive decline predated the haemorrhage, which reframes the haemorrhage as an event within a chronic arteriopathy
Obtain MRI with SWI and count and locate every microbleed, and look specifically for cortical superficial siderosis
Apply the Boston criteria version 2.0 and state the diagnosis rather than describing the findings
Exclude hypertensive arteriopathy on the distribution rule and on the blood-pressure record
Make an explicit anticoagulation decision rather than restarting by default, and record the reasoning
Refer for a non-pharmacological alternative for stroke prevention where anticoagulation is stopped
Address falls and maintain blood pressure at target, since both affect haemorrhage risk
contraindicated_actions: Do not restart or continue anticoagulation in severe probable amyloid angiopathy after an anticoagulation-associated lobar haemorrhage with disseminated siderosis
Do not substitute an antiplatelet agent as a 'safer' alternative — it also increases lobar haemorrhage risk in this substrate
Do not perform a lumbar puncture: the diagnosis is established and CSF cannot separate vascular from parenchymal amyloid
Do not attribute the haemorrhage to hypertension in a well-controlled patient with strictly lobar microbleeds
Do not leave the anticoagulation question unanswered a second time — that is how the first restart happened
key_reasoning_points: Anticoagulation did not cause this arteriopathy: seventeen lobar microbleeds and disseminated siderosis are the substrate the drug bled into, and recognising that is what turns a reflex restart into a considered decision

Disseminated cortical superficial siderosis is the strongest imaging predictor of recurrent lobar haemorrhage, and in this combination the haemorrhage risk exceeds the embolic risk that anticoagulation addresses
Left atrial appendage occlusion is the relevant alternative when anticoagulation must be abandoned in atrial fibrillation, which keeps the stroke-prevention question open rather than closing it
An antiplatelet is not a compromise position in amyloid angiopathy — it carries lobar haemorrhage risk without the embolic protection of an anticoagulant
Blood-pressure control is the single intervention that reduces both the haemorrhagic and the ischaemic risk in this patient, which makes it the priority once the antithrombotic question is settled

red_herrings.data_point: Permanent atrial fibrillation with a high stroke risk score
red_herrings.intended_effect: Makes anticoagulation appear mandatory and justifies the restart that has already happened once
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The recurrent lobar haemorrhage risk in severe probable amyloid angiopathy with disseminated siderosis exceeds the embolic benefit; the correct response is to stop the anticoagulant and refer for left atrial appendage occlusion, not to accept the risk silently

red_herrings.data_point: A haemorrhage that occurred while on apixaban
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attributes the bleed entirely to the drug, implying that careful dosing or a different agent would make anticoagulation safe again
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Seventeen strictly lobar microbleeds and disseminated siderosis predate any drug effect; the anticoagulant unmasked an underlying amyloid angiopathy, and no dose or agent removes that substrate

key_educational_points: Amyloid angiopathy is the substrate that turns an anticoagulant into a lobar haemorrhage; the drug is the trigger, not the disease
Disseminated cortical superficial siderosis is the strongest predictor of recurrent lobar haemorrhage
Left atrial appendage occlusion is the alternative when anticoagulation must be stopped in atrial fibrillation
An antiplatelet is not a safe compromise in amyloid angiopathy
